claim: Myh9 mRNA is detected at high levels throughout preimplantation development.
source: We detected high levels of Myh9 mRNA throughout preimplantation development (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Myh9 transcripts are the most abundant among NMHCs at the zygote stage (E0.5).
source: Importantly, transcripts of Myh9 are by far the most abundant among NMHCs at the zygote stage (E0.5), which suggests that Myh9 is the main NMHC paralog provided maternally.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR measurements at E0.5 shown in Figure 1A

claim: Myh9 is the main NMHC paralog provided maternally.
source: Importantly, transcripts of Myh9 are by far the most abundant among NMHCs at the zygote stage (E0.5), which suggests that Myh9 is the main NMHC paralog provided maternally.
evidence: Inferred from the high abundance of Myh9 transcripts at the zygote stage

claim: Myh10 mRNA is detected at very low levels in zygotes.
source: Myh10 mRNA is detected at very low levels in zygotes before it reaches comparable levels to Myh9 mRNA at the morula stage (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Myh10 mRNA reaches comparable levels to Myh9 mRNA at the morula stage.
source: Myh10 mRNA is detected at very low levels in zygotes before it reaches comparable levels to Myh9 mRNA at the morula stage (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Myh14 is not expressed during preimplantation stages.
source: We found that Myh14 is not expressed during preimplantation stages (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Myh14 is unlikely to play an important role in preimplantation development.
source: Since Myh14 homozygous mutant mice are viable and show no apparent defects (Ma et al., 2010), Myh14 is unlikely to play an important role in preimplantation development.
evidence: Based on citation to Ma et al., 2010 showing viable Myh14 mutants and inference from lack of expression

claim: qPCR measurements show similar trends to available mouse single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data.
source: These qPCR measurements show similar trends to available mouse single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison with published scRNA-seq data from Deng et al., 2014

claim: In humans, scRNA-seq data indicate similar expression levels between MYH9 and MYH10 during preimplantation development.
source: In humans, scRNA-seq data indicate similar expression levels between MYH9 and MYH10 during preimplantation development and, as in mice, the absence of MYH14 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on analysis of human scRNA-seq data from Yan et al., 2013

claim: In humans, MYH14 is not expressed during preimplantation development.
source: In humans, scRNA-seq data indicate similar expression levels between MYH9 and MYH10 during preimplantation development and, as in mice, the absence of MYH14 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on analysis of human scRNA-seq data from Yan et al., 2013

claim: There is conserved regulation of NMHC paralogs in mouse and human preimplantation development.
source: This points to a conserved regulation of NMHC paralogs in mouse and human preimplantation development.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of mouse and human expression patterns

claim: MYH9 protein becomes visible at the cortex of blastomeres from the zygote stage onwards.
source: At the protein level, immunostaining of MYH9 becomes visible at the cortex of blastomeres from the zygote stage onwards (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B

claim: MYH10 protein becomes detectable at the earliest at the 16-cell stage.
source: On the other hand, MYH10 becomes detectable at the earliest at the 16-cell stage (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Embryos from MYH9-GFP females show highest levels of fluorescence at the zygote stage.
source: Embryos coming from MYH9-GFP females show highest levels of fluorescence at the zygote stage, consistent with our qPCR measurement and scRNA-seq data (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D

claim: MYH9-GFP produced from the paternal allele is detected at the 4-cell stage.
source: MYH9-GFP produced from the paternal allele is detected at the 4-cell stage and increases until blastocyst stage, reaching levels comparable to blastocyst coming from MYH9-GFP females (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D

claim: MYH9 and MYH10 are the most abundant NMHCs during mouse and human preimplantation development.
source: Together, we conclude that MYH9 and MYH10 are the most abundant NMHCs during mouse and human preimplantation development and that MYH9 is heavily maternally provided at both the transcript and protein level in the mouse embryo (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from qPCR, scRNA-seq, immunostaining, and MYH9-GFP data

claim: MYH9 is heavily maternally provided at both the transcript and protein level in the mouse embryo.
source: Together, we conclude that MYH9 and MYH10 are the most abundant NMHCs during mouse and human preimplantation development and that MYH9 is heavily maternally provided at both the transcript and protein level in the mouse embryo (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from qPCR, immunostaining, and MYH9-GFP data

claim: Initial studies of Myh9 or Myh10 zygotic knockouts reported that single zygotic knockouts are able to implant.
source: Initial studies of Myh9 or Myh10 zygotic knockouts have reported that single zygotic knockouts are able to implant, suggesting they are able to form a functional blastocyst (Conti et al., 2004; Tullio et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on citations to Conti et al., 2004 and Tullio et al., 1997

claim: WT and maternal Myh10 mutants have a spherical zona pellucida.
source: WT and maternal Myh10 mutants have a spherical ZP, whereas maternal Myh9 mutants show an irregularly shaped ZP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by imaging and measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Maternal Myh9 mutants show an irregularly shaped zona pellucida.
source: WT and maternal Myh10 mutants have a spherical ZP, whereas maternal Myh9 mutants show an irregularly shaped ZP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by imaging and measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Maternal MYH9 has a previously unreported role in the formation of the zona pellucida during oogenesis.
source: This suggests a previously unreported role of contractility in the formation of the ZP during oogenesis that is mediated specifically by maternal MYH9.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of irregularly shaped ZP in maternal Myh9 mutants

claim: The abnormally shaped zona pellucida could cause long-term deformation of the embryo.
source: The abnormally shaped ZP could cause long-term deformation of the embryo, as previous studies indicate that the ZP can influence the shape of the embryo at the blastocyst stage (Kurotaki et al., 2007; Motosugi et al., 2005).
evidence: Speculation based on citations to Kurotaki et al., 2007 and Motosugi et al., 2005

claim: In WT embryos, contact angles increase from 87 ± 3° to 147 ± 2° during the 8-cell stage between the third and the fourth cleavage.
source: In WT embryos, contact angles increase from 87 ± 3° to 147 ± 2° during the 8-cell stage between the third and the fourth cleavage (mean ± SEM from the end of the last cleavage of the third wave to the first one of the fourth wave, 23 embryos, Figure 2A–B, Appendix 1—table 1–2, Figure 2—video 1), as measured previously (Maître et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by contact angle measurements from 23 WT embryos and consistent with previous studies

claim: In mzMyh9 embryos, contact angles only grow from 85 ± 2° to 125 ± 4°.
source: In mzMyh9 embryos, contact angles only grow from 85 ± 2° to 125 ± 4° (mean ± SEM, 15 embryos, Figure 2A–B, Appendix 1—table 1–2).
evidence: Supported by contact angle measurements from 15 mzMyh9 embryos

claim: The reduced ability to compact in mzMyh9 embryos is in agreement with previous measurements on heterozygous mMyh9 embryos, which generate a lower surface tension.
source: This reduced ability to compact is in agreement with previous measurements on heterozygous mMyh9 embryos, which generate a lower surface tension, and therefore cannot efficiently pull cells into closer contact (Maître et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on citation to Maître et al., 2016 showing lower surface tension in mMyh9 embryos

claim: During the 8-cell stage, mzMyh10 embryos initially grow their contacts from 87 ± 5° to 121 ± 4°, similarly to mzMyh9 embryos.
source: During the 8-cell stage, mzMyh10 embryos initially grow their contacts from 87 ± 5° to 121 ± 4°, similarly to mzMyh9 embryos (mean ± SEM, 11 embryos, Figure 2A–B, Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Supported by contact angle measurements from 11 mzMyh10 embryos

claim: mzMyh10 embryos continue to increase their contact size and reach compaction levels identical to WT embryos by the end of the 16-cell stage.
source: However, unlike mzMyh9 embryos, mzMyh10 embryos continue to increase their contact size and reach compaction levels identical to WT embryos by the end of the 16-cell stage (148 ± 4°, mean ± SEM, 11 embryos, Figure 2A–B, Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Supported by contact angle measurements from 11 mzMyh10 embryos

claim: Heterozygous mMyh9 or mMyh10 embryos show similar phenotypes to their respective homozygous counterparts.
source: Importantly, heterozygous mMyh9 or mMyh10 embryos show similar phenotypes to their respective homozygous counterparts (Figure 2B, Appendix 1—table 1–2), suggesting that maternal loss dominates for both NMHC paralogs and that the paternal allele makes little difference.
evidence: Supported by comparison of phenotypes shown in Figure 2B and Appendix 1—table 1–2

claim: Maternal loss dominates for both NMHC paralogs and the paternal allele makes little difference.
source: Importantly, heterozygous mMyh9 or mMyh10 embryos show similar phenotypes to their respective homozygous counterparts (Figure 2B, Appendix 1—table 1–2), suggesting that maternal loss dominates for both NMHC paralogs and that the paternal allele makes little difference.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between heterozygous and homozygous mutants

claim: Maternal MYH9 is essential for embryos to compact fully.
source: Together, we conclude that maternal MYH9 is essential for embryos to compact fully, whereas MYH10 only regulates the rate of compaction.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from contact angle measurements across genotypes

claim: MYH10 only regulates the rate of compaction.
source: Together, we conclude that maternal MYH9 is essential for embryos to compact fully, whereas MYH10 only regulates the rate of compaction.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from contact angle measurements showing delayed but eventual full compaction in mzMyh10 embryos

claim: The duration of the 8-cell stage is longer in embryos lacking maternal Myh9 (9.8 ± 0.5 hr) compared to WT (7.0 ± 0.3 hr).
source: We also noted that the duration of the 8-cell stage is longer in embryos lacking maternal Myh9 (9.8 ± 0.5 hr from the third to the fourth wave of cleavages, mean ± SEM, 15 embryos) as compared to WT (7.0 ± 0.3 hr, mean ± SEM, 23 embryos; Figure 2A,B, Appendix 1—tables 1–2, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: Supported by timing measurements from time-lapse imaging

claim: The duration of the fourth wave of cleavages and the ensuing 16-cell stage are similar in WT and mzMyh9 embryos.
source: This is not the case for the duration of the fourth wave of cleavages or the ensuing 16-cell stage, which are similar in these different genotypes (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: Supported by timing measurements shown in Appendix 1—table 2

claim: When reaching the blastocyst stage, mzMyh9 embryos count less than half the number of cells than WT (25.2 ± 2.8 cells vs 58.1 ± 2.9 cells).
source: Indeed, when reaching the blastocyst stage, mzMyh9 embryos count less than half the number of cells than WT (58.1 ± 2.9 cells in 23 WT embryos, as compared to 25.2 ± 2.8 cells in 15 mzMyh9 embryos, Mean ± SEM; Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Cell death was not observed in time-lapse movies of mzMyh9 embryos.
source: In the time-lapse movies, we did not observe cell death, which could, in principle, also explain a reduced cell number at the blastocyst stage.
evidence: Based on observation of time-lapse movies

claim: Reverting cleavages were observed in maternal Myh9 mutants.
source: On the other hand, we did observe reverting cleavages in maternal Myh9 mutants (Figure 2—video 3), effectively reducing cell number at the blastocyst stage.
evidence: Supported by observation in time-lapse video Figure 2—video 3

claim: Loss of MYH9 is likely to cause difficulties during cytokinesis.
source: Loss of MYH9 is likely to cause difficulties during cytokinesis (Taneja et al., 2020; Yamamoto et al., 2019), which could in turn impact cell cycle progression (Figure 2B) and explain the significant reduction in cell number in mzMyh9 embryos.
evidence: Based on citations to Taneja et al., 2020 and Yamamoto et al., 2019, and inference from observed phenotypes

claim: mzMyh10 embryos do not show any cell cycle delay and count blastocysts with the correct cell number.
source: As for mzMyh10 embryos, we do not observe any cell cycle delay and count blastocysts with the correct cell number (Figure 2B and Figure 3B), indicating that MYH9 is the primary NMHC powering cytokinesis during mouse preimplantation development.
evidence: Supported by timing and cell counting data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 3B

claim: MYH9 is the primary NMHC powering cytokinesis during mouse preimplantation development.
source: As for mzMyh10 embryos, we do not observe any cell cycle delay and count blastocysts with the correct cell number (Figure 2B and Figure 3B), indicating that MYH9 is the primary NMHC powering cytokinesis during mouse preimplantation development.
evidence: Inferred from the contrast between mzMyh9 and mzMyh10 phenotypes

claim: Periodic contractions were detected in 18/21 WT embryos.
source: While 18/21 WT embryos displayed periodic contractions, these were rarely detected in Myh9 mutants (1/15 mzMyh9 and 0/8 mMyh9 embryos) and occasionally in Myh10 mutants (3/11 mzMyh10 and 8/20 mMyh10 embryos; Figure 2G, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: Supported by PIV and Fourier analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: Periodic contractions were rarely detected in Myh9 mutants (1/15 mzMyh9 and 0/8 mMyh9 embryos).
source: While 18/21 WT embryos displayed periodic contractions, these were rarely detected in Myh9 mutants (1/15 mzMyh9 and 0/8 mMyh9 embryos) and occasionally in Myh10 mutants (3/11 mzMyh10 and 8/20 mMyh10 embryos; Figure 2G, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: Supported by PIV and Fourier analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: Periodic contractions were occasionally detected in Myh10 mutants (3/11 mzMyh10 and 8/20 mMyh10 embryos).
source: While 18/21 WT embryos displayed periodic contractions, these were rarely detected in Myh9 mutants (1/15 mzMyh9 and 0/8 mMyh9 embryos) and occasionally in Myh10 mutants (3/11 mzMyh10 and 8/20 mMyh10 embryos; Figure 2G, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: Supported by PIV and Fourier analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: Contractility is reduced after maternal loss of Myh10 and is greatly reduced following maternal loss of Myh9.
source: This suggests that contractility is reduced after maternal loss of Myh10 and is greatly reduced following maternal loss of Myh9.
evidence: Inferred from the frequency of periodic contractions across genotypes

claim: The amplitude of periodic contractions correlates with the contact angle across genotypes (Pearson's R = 0.608, p < 10−5).
source: In fact, we found that the amplitude of periodic contractions correlates with the contact angle across the genotypes we considered (Figure 2H, 75 embryos, Pearson's R = 0.608, p < 10−5, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2H and Appendix 1—table 3

claim: There is a continuum between the short-term impact of Myh9 or Myh10 loss onto contractile movements and the long-term morphogenesis.
source: This analysis across timescales reveals the continuum between the short-term impact of Myh9 or Myh10 loss onto contractile movements and the long-term morphogenesis, as previously observed for internalizing ICM cells (Maître et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between periodic contractions and contact angles, and supported by citation to Maître et al., 2016

claim: Despite showing less than half the expected cell number, mzMyh9 blastocysts show the same proportion of inner and outer cells as WT and mzMyh10 embryos.
source: Despite showing less than half the expected cell number, mzMyh9 blastocysts show the same proportion of inner and outer cells as WT and mzMyh10 embryos (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The remaining contractility in mzMyh9 embryos is sufficient to drive cell internalization or oriented cell divisions can mitigate the loss of contractility-mediated internalization.
source: This suggests that the remaining contractility is sufficient to drive cell internalization or that oriented cell divisions can mitigate the loss of contractility-mediated internalization (Korotkevich et al., 2017; Maître et al., 2016; Niwayama et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculation based on observed proportions and citations to relevant studies

claim: mzMyh10 embryos display negligible reduction in CDX2 and SOX2 levels compared to WT embryos.
source: mzMyh10 embryos display negligible reduction in CDX2 and SOX2 levels compared to WT embryos (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 3E–G

claim: mzMyh9 embryos show lower levels of CDX2 in their outer cells compared to WT embryos.
source: On the other hand, we found that mzMyh9 embryos show lower levels of CDX2 in their outer cells, as measured here and previously for mMyh9 embryos at the 16-cell stage (Figure 3F; Maître et al., 2016), and of SOX2 for inner cells compared to WT embryos (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 3F and citation to Maître et al., 2016

claim: mzMyh9 embryos show lower levels of SOX2 in inner cells compared to WT embryos.
source: On the other hand, we found that mzMyh9 embryos show lower levels of CDX2 in their outer cells, as measured here and previously for mMyh9 embryos at the 16-cell stage (Figure 3F; Maître et al., 2016), and of SOX2 for inner cells compared to WT embryos (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 3G

claim: Reduced differentiation in mzMyh9 embryos is caused in part by the presence of individual unspecified cells localized both inside and at the surface.
source: This is caused in part by the presence of individual unspecified cells localized both inside and at the surface of mzMyh9 embryos (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The correlation between the duration of the 8-cell stage and the levels of CDX2 in the TE and of SOX2 in the ICM is poor for all maternal Myh9 mutants (Pearson's R = −0.193 for CDX2 and −0.076 for SOX2, 22 embryos, p>10−2).
source: To assess whether delayed cell cycle progression may explain the reduced differentiation, we calculated the correlation between the duration of the 8-cell stage and the levels of CDX2 in the TE and of SOX2 in the ICM. This correlation is poor for all maternal Myh9 mutants (Pearson's R = −0.193 for CDX2 and −0.076 for SOX2, 22 embryos, p>10−2), which does not support reduced differentiation levels due to cell cycle delay.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of timing and differentiation marker levels

claim: Reduced differentiation levels in mzMyh9 embryos are not due to cell cycle delay.
source: To assess whether delayed cell cycle progression may explain the reduced differentiation, we calculated the correlation between the duration of the 8-cell stage and the levels of CDX2 in the TE and of SOX2 in the ICM. This correlation is poor for all maternal Myh9 mutants (Pearson's R = −0.193 for CDX2 and −0.076 for SOX2, 22 embryos, p>10−2), which does not support reduced differentiation levels due to cell cycle delay.
evidence: Inferred from the poor correlation between cell cycle duration and differentiation marker levels

claim: In WT embryos, YAP is enriched specifically in the nuclei of TE cells.
source: In WT embryos, YAP is enriched specifically in the nuclei of TE cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Hirate et al., 2013; Nishioka et al., 2009; Wicklow et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous studies

claim: YAP localization is unaffected in mzMyh10 mutants.
source: Consistent with CDX2 and SOX2 levels, YAP localization is unaffected in mzMyh10 mutants and reduced in mzMyh9 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as observed previously in mMyh9 mutants at the 16-cell stage (Maître et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: YAP localization is reduced in mzMyh9 mutants.
source: Consistent with CDX2 and SOX2 levels, YAP localization is unaffected in mzMyh10 mutants and reduced in mzMyh9 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as observed previously in mMyh9 mutants at the 16-cell stage (Maître et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Maître et al., 2016

claim: In the mouse preimplantation embryo, the nuclear localization of YAP is promoted by signals from the apical domain.
source: In the mouse preimplantation embryo, the nuclear localization of YAP is promoted by signals from the apical domain (Hirate et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on citation to Hirate et al., 2013

claim: ML7 treatment suggests that contractility may be required for apical domain formation.
source: ML7 treatment, which inhibits the myosin light chain kinase, suggests that contractility may be required for apical domain formation (Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on citation to Zhu et al., 2017

claim: mzMyh9 and mzMyh10 embryos accumulate the apical marker PRKCz at the embryo surface, as in WT.
source: However, immunostaining of apico-basal markers reveals that, as in WT, mzMyh9 and mzMyh10 embryos accumulate the apical marker PRKCz at the embryo surface (Figure 4; Hirate et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4

claim: Basolateral markers CDH1, ATP1A1, and AQP3 are enriched at basolateral membranes of WT, mzMyh9, and mzMyh10 embryos alike.
source: Also, basolateral markers such as the adhesion molecule CDH1 or members of the fluid transport machinery, such as the ATP1A1 subunit of the Na/K pump and aquaporin AQP3, are enriched at basolateral membranes of WT, mzMyh9, and mzMyh10 embryos alike (Figure 4; Barcroft et al., 2003; Barcroft et al., 2004; Dumortier et al., 2019; Stephenson et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4 and citations to previous studies

claim: MYH9-mediated contractility is required for the correct expression of lineage markers downstream of YAP but dispensable for the establishment of apico-basal polarity.
source: Together, these findings suggest that MYH9-mediated contractility is required for the correct expression of lineage markers downstream of YAP but dispensable for the establishment of apico-basal polarity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that apico-basal polarity is maintained while YAP and lineage marker levels are reduced in mzMyh9 embryos

claim: WT embryos inflate at 3.9 ± 0.5 µm2/min during lumen formation.
source: After the fifth cleavage, the growth of the blastocoel inflates and increases the projected area of WT embryos steadily at 3.9 ± 0.5 µm2/min (mean ± SEM, 20 embryos; Figure 2C, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: Supported by growth rate measurements from 20 WT embryos shown in Figure 2C

claim: mzMyh9 embryos inflate at 3.9 ± 1.0 µm2/min during lumen formation, which is similar to WT embryos.
source: During lumen formation, mzMyh9 and mzMyh10 embryos inflate at 3.9 ± 1.0 and 4.0 ± 0.5 µm2/min, respectively, which is similar to WT embryos (mean ± SEM, 9 and 7 embryos; Student's t test compared to WT p>10−2, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by growth rate measurements from 9 mzMyh9 embryos shown in Figure 2C

claim: mzMyh10 embryos inflate at 4.0 ± 0.5 µm2/min during lumen formation, which is similar to WT embryos.
source: During lumen formation, mzMyh9 and mzMyh10 embryos inflate at 3.9 ± 1.0 and 4.0 ± 0.5 µm2/min, respectively, which is similar to WT embryos (mean ± SEM, 9 and 7 embryos; Student's t test compared to WT p>10−2, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by growth rate measurements from 7 mzMyh10 embryos shown in Figure 2C

claim: Blastocoel expansion rate is unaffected in NMHC mutants.
source: This suggests that blastocoel expansion rate is unaffected in NMHC mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the similar growth rates between WT and mutant embryos

claim: The time of lumen opening in mzMyh9 embryos is not delayed compared to WT embryos.
source: Importantly, we observe that the time of lumen opening in mzMyh9 embryos is not delayed compared to WT embryos (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by timing measurements shown in Figure 2A–C

claim: Relative to the time of third cleavage, the lumen inflates on average at an earlier stage in mzMyh9 embryos than in WT.
source: In fact, relative to the time of third cleavage, the lumen inflates on average at an earlier stage in mzMyh9 embryos than in WT (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by timing measurements shown in Figure 2C

claim: Some mzMyh9 embryos begin inflating their lumen before the fifth wave of cleavages (5/11).
source: Some mzMyh9 embryos begin inflating their lumen before the fifth wave of cleavages (5/11; Figure 2—video 1), while all WT and mzMyh10 embryos begin lumen formation after the first cleavages of the fifth wave.
evidence: Supported by observation in time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2—video 1

claim: All WT and mzMyh10 embryos begin lumen formation after the first cleavages of the fifth wave.
source: Some mzMyh9 embryos begin inflating their lumen before the fifth wave of cleavages (5/11; Figure 2—video 1), while all WT and mzMyh10 embryos begin lumen formation after the first cleavages of the fifth wave.
evidence: Supported by observation in time-lapse imaging

claim: mzMyh9 embryos do not have a global delay in their development, despite their longer cell cycles, lower cell number, and impaired differentiation.
source: This argues against mzMyh9 embryos having a global delay in their development, despite their longer cell cycles, lower cell number (Figure 2B and Figure 3B), and impaired differentiation (Figure 3D,F–G).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that lumen formation is not delayed in mzMyh9 embryos

claim: Embryos with mutated maternal Myh9 alleles become less spherical than those with a WT allele.
source: Finally, when the lumen becomes sufficiently large, embryos come into contact with the ZP. 3D segmentation of blastocysts reveals that embryos with mutated maternal Myh9 alleles become less spherical than those with a WT allele (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by 3D segmentation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F

claim: The shape of the ZP of mutant embryos at the 2-cell stage correlates with the shape of embryos at the blastocyst stage (Pearson's R = −0.739, p<10−2).
source: In fact, the shape of the ZP of mutant embryos at the 2-cell stage correlates with the shape of embryos at the blastocyst stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G; 67 embryos from all genotypes combined but WT, Pearson's R = −0.739, p<10−2), which suggests that the misshapen ZP could deform the embryo.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: The misshapen ZP could deform the embryo.
source: In fact, the shape of the ZP of mutant embryos at the 2-cell stage correlates with the shape of embryos at the blastocyst stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G; 67 embryos from all genotypes combined but WT, Pearson's R = −0.739, p<10−2), which suggests that the misshapen ZP could deform the embryo.
evidence: Speculation based on correlation between ZP shape and embryo shape, and citations to previous studies

claim: The ZP can influence the shape of the blastocyst.
source: This is consistent with previous studies reporting on Myh9 mutant embryos being more deformable than WT (Maître et al., 2016) and on the influence of the ZP on the shape of the blastocyst (Kurotaki et al., 2007; Motosugi et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on citations to Kurotaki et al., 2007 and Motosugi et al., 2005

claim: Experimental deformation of the embryo was reported to affect cell fate.
source: Experimental deformation of the embryo was reported to affect cell fate (Niwayama et al., 2019; Royer et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on citations to Niwayama et al., 2019 and Royer et al., 2020

claim: In the range of deformation of the ZP observed in mutant embryos, there are weak correlations between the shape of the ZP and CDX2 or SOX2 levels.
source: In the range of deformation of the ZP observed in mutant embryos, we found weak correlations between the shape of the ZP and CDX2 or SOX2 levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–I, CDX2 in outer cells of 77 embryos from all genotypes combined but WT, Pearson's R = 0.315, p<10−2, SOX2 in the inner cells of 58 embryos, Pearson's R = 0.223, p > 10−1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–I

claim: Defects in lineage specification of maternal Myh9 mutant embryos do not simply result from the deformation of these blastocysts by their ZP.
source: This suggests that defects in lineage specification of maternal Myh9 mutant embryos do not simply result from the deformation of these blastocysts by their ZP.
evidence: Inferred from the weak correlations between ZP shape and lineage marker levels

claim: Maternal-zygotic loss of Myh9 or Myh10 has little impact on lumen formation.
source: From this multiscale analysis, we conclude that maternal-zygotic loss of Myh9 or Myh10 has little impact on lumen formation and that maternal loss of Myh9 impacts the shape of the blastocyst indirectly by its initial effect on the structure of the ZP.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from growth rate and timing measurements

claim: Maternal loss of Myh9 impacts the shape of the blastocyst indirectly by its initial effect on the structure of the ZP.
source: From this multiscale analysis, we conclude that maternal-zygotic loss of Myh9 or Myh10 has little impact on lumen formation and that maternal loss of Myh9 impacts the shape of the blastocyst indirectly by its initial effect on the structure of the ZP.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from correlation between ZP shape and blastocyst shape

claim: Reducing cell number by ¼ or ½ at the 4-cell stage results in embryos compacting with the same magnitude as control embryos.
source: Reducing cell number by ¼ or ½ at the 4-cell stage results in embryos compacting with the same magnitude and forming a lumen concomitantly to control embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C, Figure 2—video 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by measurements from fused embryos shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Reducing cell number by ¼ or ½ at the 4-cell stage results in embryos forming a lumen concomitantly to control embryos.
source: Reducing cell number by ¼ or ½ at the 4-cell stage results in embryos compacting with the same magnitude and forming a lumen concomitantly to control embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C, Figure 2—video 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by measurements from fused embryos shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Embryos with reduced cell numbers differentiate into TE and ICM identically to control embryos as far as lineage proportions and fate marker levels are concerned.
source: Also, embryos with reduced cell numbers differentiate into TE and ICM identically to control embryos as far as lineage proportions and fate marker levels are concerned (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C–E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data from fused embryos shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C–E

claim: The morphogenesis and lineage specification defects observed in maternal Myh9 mutants are not likely to result simply from cytokinesis defects and their impact on cell number.
source: Therefore, the morphogenesis and lineage specification defects observed in maternal Myh9 mutants are not likely to result simply from cytokinesis defects and their impact on cell number.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that fused embryos with reduced cell number do not show similar defects

claim: MYH9 plays a critical role in setting global cell contractility on short and long timescales in order to effectively drive compaction, cytokinesis, and lineage specification.
source: Together, these analyses reveal the critical role of MYH9 in setting global cell contractility on short and long timescales in order to effectively drive compaction, cytokinesis, and lineage specification.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiscale analysis of mzMyh9 phenotypes

claim: The function of MYH10 during early blastocyst morphogenesis is less prominent compared to MYH9.
source: Comparably, the function of MYH10 during early blastocyst morphogenesis is less prominent.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of mzMyh9 and mzMyh10 phenotypes

claim: The preimplantation embryo primarily relies on the maternal pools of MYH9.
source: Importantly, the similarity of maternal homozygous and maternal heterozygous mutants indicates that the preimplantation embryo primarily relies on the maternal pools of MYH9.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between maternal homozygous and heterozygous mutants

claim: Maternally provided MYH9 is the main NMHC powering actomyosin contractility during early preimplantation development.
source: We conclude that maternally provided MYH9 is the main NMHC powering actomyosin contractility during early preimplantation development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the dominant phenotype of maternal Myh9 loss

claim: mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos fail most attempts of cytokinesis.
source: Nested time-lapse revealed that mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos fail most attempts of cytokinesis (Figure 5A, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—video 1

claim: mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos show increased cell cycle durations, which are more severe than those for mzMyh9 embryos.
source: In addition to failed cytokinesis, mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos show increased cell cycle durations, which are more severe than those for mzMyh9 embryos (Figure 5A–B, Appendix 1—table 1–2).
evidence: Supported by timing measurements shown in Figure 5A–B and Appendix 1—table 1–2

claim: mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos have only 2.9 ± 0.5 cells when reaching the blastocyst stage.
source: This results in mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos with only 2.9 ± 0.5 cells when reaching the blastocyst stage (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 6B

claim: mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos occasionally develop into blastocyst-stage embryos consisting of only one single cell (1/8 embryos).
source: In fact, they occasionally develop into blastocyst-stage embryos consisting of only one single cell (1/8 embryos).
evidence: Supported by observation from 8 mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos

claim: Contact angles for mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos cap at 117 ± 4° compared to 147 ± 2° for WT.
source: Of those which succeed in dividing at least once, compaction after the third cleavage is weak with contact angles for mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos capping at 117 ± 4° compared to 147 ± 2° for WT (mean ± SEM, 3 and 23 embryos; Figure 5B, Appendix 1—table 1, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by contact angle measurements from 3 mzMyh9;mzMyh10 and 23 WT embryos

claim: Periodic contractions are undetectable in any of the double mutants analyzed.
source: Consistent with previous observations, periodic contractions are undetectable in any of the double mutants that we analyzed (Figure 5D–E, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: Supported by PIV and Fourier analysis shown in Figure 5D–E

claim: Double maternal-zygotic Myh9 and Myh10 mutants generate extremely weak contractile forces compared to WT and single maternal-zygotic Myh9 or Myh10 mutants.
source: Together, this indicates that double maternal-zygotic Myh9 and Myh10 mutants generate extremely weak contractile forces compared to WT and single maternal-zygotic Myh9 or Myh10 mutants.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from contact angle measurements and absence of periodic contractions

claim: CDX2 is present in 5/7 mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos as compared to all the 23 WT embryos analyzed.
source: When investigating fate specification (Figure 6), CDX2 is present in 5/7 embryos as compared to all the 23 WT embryos we analyzed (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6F

claim: SOX2 is only detected when mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos succeed in internalizing at least one cell.
source: SOX2 is only detected when embryos succeed in internalizing at least one cell (Figure 6A,C–E and G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A,C–E and G

claim: No maternal Myh9;Myh10 mutant embryo consisting of only two cells contained an inner cell.
source: No maternal Myh9;Myh10 mutant embryo consisting of only two cells contained an inner cell, half of embryos with 3–5 cells contained a single inner cell, and all embryos with six cells or more contained inner cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by cell counting and position data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Half of maternal Myh9;Myh10 mutant embryos with 3–5 cells contained a single inner cell.
source: No maternal Myh9;Myh10 mutant embryo consisting of only two cells contained an inner cell, half of embryos with 3–5 cells contained a single inner cell, and all embryos with six cells or more contained inner cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by cell counting and position data shown in Figure 6D

claim: All maternal Myh9;Myh10 mutant embryos with six cells or more contained inner cells.
source: No maternal Myh9;Myh10 mutant embryo consisting of only two cells contained an inner cell, half of embryos with 3–5 cells contained a single inner cell, and all embryos with six cells or more contained inner cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by cell counting and position data shown in Figure 6D

claim: The levels of CDX2 in outer cells of mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos are reduced compared to WT embryos.
source: Moreover, the levels of CDX2 in outer cells are reduced compared to WT embryos, as observed previously for single maternal-zygotic Myh9 mutants.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 6F

claim: YAP is enriched in the nucleus of outer cells of mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos, albeit at lower levels than in WT.
source: Consistently, YAP is enriched in the nucleus of outer cells, albeit at lower levels than in WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The apical marker PRKCz, F-actin, the cell-cell adhesion molecule CDH1, and members of the fluid-pumping machinery ATP1A1 and AQP3 are correctly apico-basally polarized in double mutants.
source: As for single mutants, the apical marker PRKCz, F-actin, the cell-cell adhesion molecule CDH1, and members of the fluid-pumping machinery ATP1A1 and AQP3 are correctly apico-basally polarized in double mutants (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7

claim: mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos can initiate differentiation into TE.
source: The presence of CDX2, nuclear YAP, and the correct organization of apico-basal polarity suggest that mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos can initiate differentiation into TE, the epithelium responsible for making the blastocoel.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of CDX2, nuclear YAP, and apico-basal polarity markers

claim: mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos can create de novo a functional polarized epithelium.
source: The ability of mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos to create de novo a functional polarized epithelium is further supported by the fact that they can eventually proceed with polarized fluid accumulation and create a blastocoel (Figure 5A, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by observation of fluid accumulation in time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—video 1

claim: mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos are not delayed to initiate lumen formation despite their extended cell cycles.
source: As observed in single maternal Myh9 mutants, mzMyh9;mzMyh10 embryos are not delayed to initiate lumen formation despite their extended cell cycles (Figure 5C, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by timing measurements shown in Figure 5C

claim: mzMyh9;mzMyh10 mutant embryos grow at rates that are similar to WT ones (5.8 ± 1.5 and 3.9 ± 0.5 µm2/min).
source: Also, we measure that mutant embryos grow at rates that are similar to WT ones (5.8 ± 1.5 and 3.9 ± 0.5 µm2/min, mean ± SEM, 5 and 20 embryos, Student's t test p>10−2; Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by growth rate measurements from 5 mutant and 20 WT embryos shown in Figure 5C

claim: Contractility does not influence the initial growth rate of the blastocoel.
source: This indicates that contractility does not influence the initial growth rate of the blastocoel and that blastocoel formation does not require powerful actomyosin contractility.
evidence: Inferred from the similar growth rates between WT and double mutant embryos

claim: Blastocoel formation does not require powerful actomyosin contractility.
source: This indicates that contractility does not influence the initial growth rate of the blastocoel and that blastocoel formation does not require powerful actomyosin contractility.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of double mutants with extremely weak contractility to form a blastocoel

claim: Maternal contributions predominantly set the contractility for preimplantation development.
source: Finally, we measure similar metrics for all single and double heterozygous Myh9 and Myh10 mutant embryos (Figure 5, Figure 6, Appendix 1—table 1), indicating once again that maternal contributions predominantly set the contractility for preimplantation development.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between homozygous and heterozygous mutants

claim: After the maternal loss of both Myh9 and Myh10, contractility is almost entirely abolished.
source: We conclude that after the maternal loss of both Myh9 and Myh10, contractility is almost entirely abolished.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the severe phenotypes of double mutants

claim: The effect of double maternal loss of Myh9 and Myh10 is much stronger than that after the loss of maternal MYH9 only.
source: This effect is much stronger than that after the loss of maternal MYH9 only and suggests that, in single maternal Myh9 mutants, MYH10 can compensate significantly, which we would not anticipate from our previous single mzMyh10 knockout analysis.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of single and double mutant phenotypes

claim: In single maternal Myh9 mutants, MYH10 can compensate significantly.
source: This effect is much stronger than that after the loss of maternal MYH9 only and suggests that, in single maternal Myh9 mutants, MYH10 can compensate significantly, which we would not anticipate from our previous single mzMyh10 knockout analysis.
evidence: Inferred from the much stronger phenotype of double mutants compared to single Myh9 mutants

claim: Despite MYH9 being the main engine of preimplantation actomyosin contractility, MYH10 ensures a substantial part of blastocyst morphogenesis in the absence of MYH9.
source: Therefore, despite MYH9 being the main engine of preimplantation actomyosin contractility, MYH10 ensures a substantial part of blastocyst morphogenesis in the absence of MYH9.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the comparison of single and double mutant phenotypes

claim: Embryos without maternal MYH9 and MYH10 can fail all successive cleavages when reaching the time of the blastocyst stage (18/53 embryos).
source: Embryos without maternal MYH9 and MYH10 can fail all successive cleavages when reaching the time of the blastocyst stage (18/53 embryos, all Myh9 and Myh10 mutant genotypes combined across seven experiments; Figure 8A, Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: Supported by observation from 53 double mutant embryos across seven experiments

claim: In single-celled embryos, multiple cleavage attempts at intervals of 10–20 hr can be observed.
source: In single-celled embryos, multiple cleavage attempts at intervals of 10–20 hr can be observed, suggesting that the cell cycle is still operational in those embryos (Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by observation in time-lapse video Figure 5—video 1

claim: The cell cycle is still operational in single-celled embryos.
source: In single-celled embryos, multiple cleavage attempts at intervals of 10–20 hr can be observed, suggesting that the cell cycle is still operational in those embryos (Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of multiple cleavage attempts and presence of multiple large nuclei

claim: Single-celled embryos contain multiple large nuclei, indicative of preserved genome replication.
source: This is further supported by the presence of multiple large nuclei in single-celled embryos, indicative of preserved genome replication (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8C

claim: Giant nuclei in single-celled embryos contain CDX2 and YAP, but no SOX2.
source: Interestingly, these giant nuclei contain CDX2 and YAP, but no SOX2, suggesting that, in addition to the cell cycle, the lineage specification program is still partially operational (Figure 8C–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8C–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: In addition to the cell cycle, the lineage specification program is still partially operational in single-celled embryos.
source: Interestingly, these giant nuclei contain CDX2 and YAP, but no SOX2, suggesting that, in addition to the cell cycle, the lineage specification program is still partially operational (Figure 8C–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the presence of CDX2 and YAP but absence of SOX2 in nuclei of single-celled embryos

claim: At the time of blastocoel formation, single-celled maternal Myh9 and Myh10 mutant embryos begin to swell to sizes comparable to normal blastocysts.
source: Strikingly, we also observed that at the time of blastocoel formation, single-celled maternal Myh9 and Myh10 mutant embryos begin to swell to sizes comparable to normal blastocysts (Figure 8A–B, Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging and growth measurements shown in Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—video 1

claim: Single-celled embryos form, within their cytoplasm, tens of fluid-filled vacuolar compartments, which can inflate into structures comparable in size to the blastocoel.
source: Single-celled embryos then form, within their cytoplasm, tens of fluid-filled vacuolar compartments, which can inflate into structures comparable in size to the blastocoel (Figure 8A and C, Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8A and C and Figure 8—video 1

claim: The membrane of cytoplasmic vacuoles in single-celled embryos contains the fluid pumping machinery ATP1A1 and AQP3.
source: The membrane of these cytoplasmic vacuoles contains the fluid pumping machinery ATP1A1 and AQP3, which is specific of basolateral membranes in multicellular embryos of all considered genotypes (Figure 7; Barcroft et al., 2003; Barcroft et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7 and citations to Barcroft et al., 2003 and 2004

claim: Single-celled embryos are able to establish apico-basal polarity and to direct fluid pumping into a basolateral compartment despite the absence of neighbouring cells.
source: This indicates that single-celled embryos are able to establish apico-basal polarity and to direct fluid pumping into a basolateral compartment despite the absence of neighbouring cells.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of basolateral markers on vacuole membranes

claim: The growth rates of single-celled embryos are comparable to those of multiple-celled mutant embryos or WT (4.1 ± 0.8, 5.8 ± 1.5, and 3.9 ± 0.5 µm2/min).
source: When measuring the growth rates of single-celled embryos, we found that they are comparable to the ones of multiple-celled mutant embryos or WT (4.1 ± 0.8, 5.8 ± 1.5, and 3.9 ± 0.5 µm2/min, mean ± SEM, 4, 5, and 20 embryos, Student's t test p > 10−2 ; Figure 8B), indicating that they are able to accumulate fluid as fast as embryos composed of multiple cells.
evidence: Supported by growth rate measurements from 4 single-celled, 5 multiple-celled mutant, and 20 WT embryos shown in Figure 8B

claim: Single-celled embryos are able to accumulate fluid as fast as embryos composed of multiple cells.
source: When measuring the growth rates of single-celled embryos, we found that they are comparable to the ones of multiple-celled mutant embryos or WT (4.1 ± 0.8, 5.8 ± 1.5, and 3.9 ± 0.5 µm2/min, mean ± SEM, 4, 5, and 20 embryos, Student's t test p > 10−2 ; Figure 8B), indicating that they are able to accumulate fluid as fast as embryos composed of multiple cells.
evidence: Inferred from the similar growth rates between single-celled and multi-celled embryos

claim: Single-celled embryos are able to initiate TE differentiation and display some attributes of epithelial function.
source: Therefore, single-celled embryos are able to initiate TE differentiation and display some attributes of epithelial function.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the presence of CDX2, YAP, apico-basal polarity markers, and fluid accumulation

claim: The developmental program entailing morphogenesis and lineage specification carries on independently of successful cleavages.
source: Together, this further indicates that the developmental program entailing morphogenesis and lineage specification carries on independently of successful cleavages.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that single-celled embryos can differentiate and accumulate fluid on schedule

claim: Fused single-celled embryos retain a TE phenotype with high CDX2 and low SOX2 levels.
source: The nuclei from the fused cells displayed high CDX2 and low SOX2 levels, which indicates that fused embryos retain a TE phenotype (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E

claim: Single-celled embryos resulting from cell fusion grew in size at rates similar to those of control embryos (3.3 ± 0.4 and 3.7 ± 0.4 µm2/min).
source: Moreover, similarly to single-celled embryos resulting from the loss of contractility, single-celled embryos resulting from cell fusion grew in size at rates similar to those of control embryos while forming large fluid-filled vacuoles (3.3 ± 0.4 and 3.7 ± 0.4 µm2/min, 7 and 8 embryos, Student's t test p > 10−2; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B, Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: Supported by growth rate measurements from 7 fused and 8 control embryos shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: Single-celled embryos resulting from cell fusion form large fluid-filled vacuoles.
source: Moreover, similarly to single-celled embryos resulting from the loss of contractility, single-celled embryos resulting from cell fusion grew in size at rates similar to those of control embryos while forming large fluid-filled vacuoles (3.3 ± 0.4 and 3.7 ± 0.4 µm2/min, 7 and 8 embryos, Student's t test p > 10−2; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B, Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and Figure 8—video 2

claim: The initiation of fluid accumulation and its rate during blastocoel morphogenesis can rely entirely on transcellular transport and are independent from cell-cell contacts and its associated paracellular transport.
source: This further confirms that the initiation of fluid accumulation and its rate during blastocoel morphogenesis can rely entirely on transcellular transport and are independent from cell-cell contacts and its associated paracellular transport.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that fused single-celled embryos accumulate fluid at normal rates

claim: MYH9 is the major NMHC powering sufficient actomyosin contractility for blastocyst morphogenesis.
source: Together, our experiments with single and double maternal-zygotic NMHC knockout embryos reveal that, while MYH9 is the major NMHC powering sufficient actomyosin contractility for blastocyst morphogenesis, MYH10 can significantly compensate the effect of MYH9 loss onto cytokinesis and compaction.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of single and double mutant phenotypes

claim: MYH10 can significantly compensate the effect of MYH9 loss onto cytokinesis and compaction.
source: Together, our experiments with single and double maternal-zygotic NMHC knockout embryos reveal that, while MYH9 is the major NMHC powering sufficient actomyosin contractility for blastocyst morphogenesis, MYH10 can significantly compensate the effect of MYH9 loss onto cytokinesis and compaction.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the much stronger phenotype of double mutants compared to single Myh9 mutants

claim: Even blastocyst-stage embryos made out of a single cell can proceed with the preimplantation program in a timely fashion.
source: Mutant and fused embryos also reveal that even blastocyst-stage embryos made out of a single cell can proceed with the preimplantation program in a timely fashion, as they differentiate into TE and build features of the blastocyst, such as the inflation of fluid-containing compartments.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of single-celled mutant and fused embryos

claim: Single-celled embryos differentiate into TE and build features of the blastocyst, such as the inflation of fluid-containing compartments.
source: Mutant and fused embryos also reveal that even blastocyst-stage embryos made out of a single cell can proceed with the preimplantation program in a timely fashion, as they differentiate into TE and build features of the blastocyst, such as the inflation of fluid-containing compartments.
evidence: Supported by observations of CDX2 expression, apico-basal polarity, and fluid accumulation in single-celled embryos

claim: Myosin mutants and fused embryos reveal that the developmental program entailing morphogenesis and lineage specification carries on independently of successful cell division.
source: Finally, myosin mutants and fused embryos reveal that the developmental program entailing morphogenesis and lineage specification carries on independently of successful cleavages. This further demonstrates the remarkable regulative capacities of the early mammalian embryo.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that single-celled embryos can differentiate and accumulate fluid on schedule

claim: The early mammalian embryo has remarkable regulative capacities.
source: Finally, myosin mutants and fused embryos reveal that the developmental program entailing morphogenesis and lineage specification carries on independently of successful cleavages. This further demonstrates the remarkable regulative capacities of the early mammalian embryo.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of single-celled embryos to proceed with development
